name: git blame
shortDescription: Show what revision and author last modified each line of a file. Essential for understanding why code was written a certain way.
detailedDescription:
The `git blame` command annotates each line of a file with the commit hash, author, and date of the last change. Despite its name, it's not about assigning blame — it's about understanding context.

When you encounter unfamiliar code, `git blame` tells you who wrote it and when, which helps you find the commit message explaining the reasoning. It's one of the most valuable debugging tools: you can trace any line back to the exact commit and PR that introduced it.

For lines that were moved or copied from other files, the `-C` flag can detect the original source, showing you the true origin of the code rather than the commit that moved it.

parameters.description: Restrict the annotation to a range of lines. Accepts line numbers or regex patterns.
Detect lines copied from other files. Use -CCC for more aggressive detection across all files in the same commit.
Ignore whitespace changes when finding the responsible commit. Prevents formatting-only commits from taking blame.
Show the author's email instead of name.
Only show blame for changes made after the given date.

examples.title: Blame a whole file
examples.description: See who last modified each line.

examples.title: Blame specific lines
examples.description: Focus on a specific section of the file.
examples.code:
# Lines 10 to 25:
git blame -L 10,25 src/auth.js

# From a function name to end of block:
git blame -L '/function login/,/^}/' src/auth.js

examples.title: Ignore whitespace changes
examples.description: Don't let formatting commits obscure the real author.
examples.code:
git blame -w src/auth.js

# Now a commit that only re-indented code won't
# take blame from the original author

commonMistakes.text: Despite the name, `git blame` is a debugging tool, not a finger-pointing tool. Use it to understand code context, find related commits, and locate the right person to ask questions.
Most editors (VS Code with GitLens, IntelliJ) have inline blame annotations. They show blame info right next to each line without running the command.
Large code reformatting commits will 'take blame' for every reformatted line. Use `.git-blame-ignore-revs` (Git 2.23+) to exclude specific commits from blame results.
